This is **misère Nim** (the player taking the last object *loses*), so I use the classical optimal strategy for misère Nim:

1. **Endgame rule (0 or 1 piles with more than one object):** Move so the opponent is left with an **odd** number of single-object piles. With exactly one "big" pile of size `n` and `k` single-object piles: reduce the big pile to 0 if `k` is odd, otherwise reduce it to 1. (If all piles are ≤ 1, just take one object — the position's outcome is already determined.)
2. **Normal Nim rule (≥ 2 piles larger than 1):** Compute the nim-sum `s = XOR` of all piles. If `s ≠ 0`, find a pile where `pile ^ s < pile` and reduce it to `pile ^ s`, leaving nim-sum 0. This is provably optimal because the misère exception only matters once fewer than two piles exceed size 1.
3. **Losing positions (nim-sum 0):** No move wins against perfect play, so take 1 from the largest pile to prolong the game and maximize the chance of an opponent mistake.

This is perfect play, runs in O(4) time, and every branch is guarded so a legal move string is always returned.
kimi_k3/002: The strategy for this policy is misère Nim theory: positions where every pile has at most 1 object are losing (P-positions) when the number of singleton piles is odd; otherwise a position with a pile larger than 1 is losing exactly when the XOR (nim-sum) is zero. The policy enumerates a handful of candidate moves per pile — the classic nim-move that zeroes the XOR, plus reducing a large pile to 0 or 1 to fix parity in the all-singletons endgame — and picks the first candidate that hands the opponent a losing position. If the position itself is already losing (or no candidate works, which cannot happen on a winning position), it falls back to the first legal move, guaranteeing a legal output string every time. All of this runs in O(4·candidates) time, far below the 1-second limit.
kimi_k3/003:
This is **misère Nim** (taking the last object *loses*), which has a well-known perfect-play solution that differs from normal Nim only in the endgame:

**P-positions (losing for the player to move) in misère Nim are exactly:**
1. All piles have size ≤ 1 with an **odd** number of size-1 piles.
2. At least one pile has size ≥ 2 and the **nim-sum (XOR) is zero**.

So my policy is:
- **Exactly one pile bigger than 1:** reduce that pile to 0 or 1 — whichever leaves an **odd** number of 1-piles for the opponent (this is the key misère correction; the "normal Nim" move here is always wrong).
- **Only 0/1 piles remain:** take a whole 1-pile (wins iff the count of 1s was even).
- **Otherwise (≥2 big piles):** if nim-sum ≠ 0, play the classic Nim move — pick a pile where `pile XOR nimsum < pile` and reduce it to `pile XOR nimsum`. This always leaves a misère P-position.
- **Theoretically lost (nim-sum = 0):** use an anti-imperfect-opponent heuristic — if possible, hand the opponent a "single big pile" position, where the normal-Nim move is *always* a blunder under misère rules; otherwise take 1 from the largest pile to prolong the game.

A fallback scan guarantees a legal move string is always returned (no disqualification). Runtime is O(4) — trivially fast.

This is **misère Nim** (taking the last object *loses*), so I use Bouton's classic misère-Nim theorem for perfect play:

- **All piles have size ≤ 1:** the position is losing only when an *odd* number of singleton piles remains. I remove one whole singleton pile, which leaves an odd number of singletons to the opponent whenever possible (forcing them to eventually take the last one).
- **Exactly one pile has size > 1:** this is always a winning position. I reduce the big pile to either 0 or 1 (whichever leaves an *odd* number of size-1 piles), handing the opponent a lost endgame.
- **Two or more piles have size > 1:** misère Nim coincides with normal Nim here. I compute the XOR (nim-sum) of all piles; if nonzero, I reduce a pile `p` to `p ^ s`, making the XOR zero — a losing position for the opponent. If the XOR is already zero, the position is theoretically lost against perfect play, so I remove just one object from the largest pile to prolong the game and maximize the opponent's chances to make a mistake.

Every branch always yields a legal move, and the strategy is provably optimal (never loses from a winning position).
